speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In the absence of the
Minister of Finance, who unavoidably is still detained at his house, I move, Mr. Chairman, that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Acting Minister of Fisheries) moved the third reading of Bill No. 6, to amend the Fish Inspection Act-.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. S3, to amend the act of incorporation of the Frontier College.
On section- 1-Power to confer degrees.
Would the minister explain the bill?

In the year 1922 parliament passed an act to incorporate the Frontier College, by chapter 77 of the statutes of that year. The objects of this college were defined in section six of the statute, as follows:
(a) To promote education among Canadian working men and women and Canadian immigrants; -(b) To promote higher educational training and instruction for teachers and social workers among Canadian working men and women and Canadian immigrants.
The objects were very praiseworthy indeed, but under section ten of the act the college was authorized to confer degrees. The college has recently applied to the government of the province of Ontario to be brought under the operation of the Education Act of Ontario and to secure certain

Royal Canadian Mounted Police
rights, privileges and emoluments which may be conferred under that provincial statute. In order that the college might be brought under that statute an agreement was entered into on the nineteenth day of December, 1931, between the Frontier College and His Majesty the King in the right of the province of Ontario as represented by the Minister of Education for Ontario. One provision of the agreement was that section ten of the act of incorporation should be repealed, and so at the request of the government of Ontario concurred in by the Frontier College, I am simply asking by this bill that section ten be repealed in order that this college, which was incorporated by a federal statute, may be brought under the operation of the Education Act of Ontario. All parties have agreed, and I have formal agreements signed to that effect.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act to provide for the appointment of a deputy commissioner, and the employment of extra constables in emergencies, and to make further provisions respecting the counting of service in the great war and in the civil service and customs-excise preventive service by officers and constables, for the purposes of pension.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as is pretty generally known, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have now entered into agreements-probably I should say the government has entered into agreements on their behalf-with the three prairie provinces and the three maritime provinces to take over the ordinary provincial police forces of those six provinces. The police forces of the provinces are being consolidated with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The agreements in respect to which these forces are taken over are practically the same, with the exception of soipe very slight variations. There is a fixed sum of so much per man allowed as payment by the provinces to the federal government. Then there is a fixed amount for expenses in connection with the transportation of prisoners and the like.
These agreements are all based on the Saskatchewan agreement passed three years ago. In the act authorizing the Saskatchewan agreement there is provision for the inclusion

of other provinces. In the view of the commissioner commanding the force it is necessary to have a deputy commissioner to assist him in his work. That is the main object of the present bill, but in addition there are other minor proposals. The bill which will be introduced is quite long, and by reason of the amalgamation a great many amendments have been made necessary. As a result of the amalgamation there will be a considerable saving to the government of Canada, brought about by the abolition of double overhead which has existed heretofore in all the provinces affected, and particularly in those in the west. When the estimate for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is before the house-and I expect it will be either to-morrow or the next day

I shall give the details of the proposed expenditures, and I think I shall be able to satisfy the house that compared with the expenditures in the past there will be a very large saving in expenses in the administration of the force.
I think that is all I need explain at this time.
Can the minister tell us what increase there will be if the amalgamation of the various forces becomes effective?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: An increase in what?
In the personnel of the force?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the personnel will be in the neighbourhood of 2,000.
But the 2,000 will not represent the increase in the force brought about by the amalgamation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; the force was about 1,250 strong; it was increased by 200 or 250 last December. The full increase will bring the whole force up to about 2,000. However I shall have exact information when we are considering the estimate.
That is for the six provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I must remind hon. members that we are not in committee.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.

Have any representations been made by the province of British Columbia?

Royal Canadian Mounted Police

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. During last summer and autumn there were negotiations. Indeed, they were continued until quite recently this spring. I was under the impression that similar arrangements would be made with the province of British Columbia, but up to the present time that province has not agreed to come in. Within the last four or five weeks I have received communications from that province, but at least for the present they have rather definitely refused. They say they will maintain their own constabulary at the present time.
Does the same situation prevail in regard to Ontario and Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; they have not come in.
Is there any arrangement in the agreement providing for the taking over of the constables now employed by the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. All the constables
now employed will' not be required in the force. As my hon. friend knows, however, in the force there is a record of the work hitherto performed by each constable, and they are being selected having regard to their services, their adaptability and their past record. Speaking from memory, I will say there were 115 in the Manitoba force, and 85 have been taken over. The same proportion would follow in regard to the other provinces.

In regard to seniority, will the old members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in the various provinces affected by this legislation have seniority over the new members of the old provincial police forces now being taken in?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the old members
will continue to hold their seniority. However, I should like to give a more definite statement when the estimate is before the house.
There is no reduction in the number of constables employed in the various provinces, as a result of the forces being taken over by the federal authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; I do not think there will be any reduction in the number.

Will the
customs-excise preventive officers be reengaged at the same salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They will be engaged as
enlisted men at the regular pay of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. A list of preventive officers has been prepared by the Department of National Revenue. It is on the recommendation of that department they have been taken in. I believe about half the staff of the preventive services will be absorbed in the mounted police; the rest will not be required.
How many of the provincial police in the province of New Brunswick have been brought in under this service? Probably the minister would prefer to answer under the estimate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should think about
ninety per cent.

In the province of New
Brunswick there is a difference between provincial police and constables.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, there is in every
province.

Yes. Two years ago the
provincial police of New Brunswick were put under a pension system. Will the pensions of those drafted into the Royal Canadian Mounted Police begin two years ago, or only from the time they were drafted in?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In each province the
provincial government must make good any deficiency in regard to the pension fund. The only province that has undertaken to do so is Saskatchewan. For instance, in Alberta the fund which has been accumulated by the province up to the present time is not sufficient to carry the pensions in force in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Unless Alberta is prepared to pay the additional amount, the pensions will have to be reduced to bring them into harmony with the amount of money that is now available in the hands of the province. The provinces are to hand over such funds as they have accumulated for the purpose of pensioning their own men in the new force, but only so far as the funds will extend. In the agreement with Saskatchewan the province has undertaken to pay it all; their men will be placed upon the same plane as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in respect to pensions. The other provinces have not yet agreed to do so; they may eventually. But the expense of doing so will have to be borne by the provinces.

Will the time served in the provincial forces be counted as service in the new force?

Royal Canadian Mounted Police

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, if the necessary amount of money is forthcoming it will be.
Is a specific establishment to be provided for each province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. A plan is being
worked out by the commissioner to carry out in each province under the mounted police the scheme which heretofore has been working in the prairie provinces only. There will be a headquarters in each province, and I suppose there will be various posts according to the localities that are deemed most desirable.

Then the service
will be interchangeable?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Oh yes; that is one of
the merits of the system we believe.

Under this agreement will
the same number of police be maintained in Alberta? I understand from letters I have received from High River that the police station at that point has been closed, although located there for forty-five years. The people are rather alarmed, and an effort is being made to have it reopened. Will the number of police to be maintained in the province be reduced compared with the number of provincial police formerly?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, there will be practically the same number in every province as heretofore. With regard to High River, I am sorry to say it is the intention to close the post. These posts are selected by the provincial administration, and Edmonton has advised us that the High River post should not be maintained any longer.

The provincial government
has advised that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

The minister stated that in some instances the amount of the pension fund standing to the credit of the provincial police would not be sufficient to carry out the agreement which these men had with their respective provinces. These men having made a contract with the provincial authorities, it seems to me very unfair that they should be transferred to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the provincial governments relieved of the responsibility of carrying out their bargains. Apparently the men because of this transfer are going to suffer after having contributed their share to the provincial pension fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I fancy it is a matter between the men and the provinces. I under-

stand that practically all the men are in favour of the arrangement. They do not look to this government to make it good.
Naturally not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is purely an actuarial
matter, and the amount can be definitely ascertained.
Quite.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But to pay the scale of
pensions payable to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would require a greater amount than is now in the hands of the provincial governments. We cannot bind the provincial governments to make up that amount. Saskatchewan has done so; Alberta and Manitoba have not done so as yet. However, that is a matter between the former constabulary of the provinces and the provincial governments. It is now under consideration, and I think in the case of one province there is only a difference between them of $20,000.

The minister does not
state the amount of money they will receive from the provinces. Will it be less than the amount required to carry out the agreement which the provincial police had with their provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It will carry out the
agreement they had with their provinces, but it will not pay the pensions payable to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

Then I withdraw my
objection.

What is the scale of
pension in each case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is higher in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

What rates of pay were
the men receiving under the provinces, and what will they receive under the dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I know the policemen
get $2 a day and certain allowances. I do not know what they got from the provinces. We agree to maintain, say, 150 men at $1,000 a man, and we receive from the province $150,000; in addition we receive the actual expenses in connection with the transportation of prisoners and the like. In some cases that has been fixed at a definite sum, but in the case of Saskatchewan we have had to do a lot of accounting, and we obtain the actual expense that we incur. It would be far better if we could arrive at a definite sum in each case. Last year we received from Saskatchewan $25,000 for the transport and care of

Royal Canadian Mounted Police
prisoners. We have fixed a definite sum with Alberta of $50,000, and I think the same with respect to Manitoba. Saskatchewan is now anxious to have a definite sum fixed in regard to its prisoners, but we have not yet been able to agree upon an amount.

Does this legislation cover
the amalgamation, if I may so call it, of the customs preventive service with the mounted police?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, this legislation does not.
Is it the taking over by the mounted police of the entire preventive service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This legislation does not
cover it; that is done by order in council under the act which authorizes rearrangement of departments of government. This provides for the preventive service in this respect, that time served heretofore in the preventive service shall be counted to the credit of these men when they join the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
For pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I was under the impression
that a large number of employees of the preventive service were on a purely temporary basis, and consequently were not entitled to pensions. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are some temporaries no doubt, and they are not entitled to pension.

They were not under the
Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A lot of them were not.
A great many of them are going to be let out of the service as unnecessary.

Has the minister some
kind of statement to make as to the procedure to be followed with respect to employees of the customs preventive service generally? I am asking that question because I have heard from Quebec that a number of former employees are being let out of the service, and are not being given an opportunity to join the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Whether they are not being given that opportunity because they are too old, incompetent, or for some other reason I do not know. Perhaps the minister could make a statement with regard to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think perhaps that is the reason-that they are too old, or some of them may be incompetent. At all events,
they have been selected on their records with the department by the officials of the Department of National Defence. Then these names, which were approved by that department, were submitted to the commissioner of the mounted police, and I think to-morrow I will be able to answer the question which more immediately concerns my hon. friend and which is on the order paper, as to the names of those in the province of Quebec who are being retained. I think there are fifty names on the list. I should have it here to-day, but I left it in my office. I will bring it to-morrow, and the names of the fifty selected are all given.
On what is this selection based?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On the records in the Department of National Defence. The selection vras made by that department and the names were submitted to the commissioner.
Have you that for every province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the system for all the provinces.
Will you have a list of the selections in all the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That list has not been compiled as yet; the selection has not been completed.
What is to become of the people who have been in the service for some considerable length of time? Have they been given notice or a gratuity in lieu of notice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I assume they will be treated as - other officials of the service are treated. Temporary employees will be allowed to retire on the terms applied to similar retirements in other departments. I do not know just what they are. Those who are entitled to retirement allowance will receive it, but as a means of economy as much as anything we have decided not to take over all the members of the service. We do not require them all, and in that way a very large saving will be made.

Under the general act or regulations ten years service is required before any return is made in connection with superannuation. A person leaving the service before completing ten years does not get back the five per cent he has put in. Under the regulations adopted two or three years ago the customs preventive service was brought under the pension system. Some of these men will be let out under this reorganization. Would the minister look into the matter and

Royal Canadian Mounted Police
let us know later on, if he has not the information now, whether these men will lose the amount they have paid into the pension fund, or whether that money will be returned to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will look into the matter. I cannot say offhand, but they will be given whatever is provided by the law.
If I am not mistaken there is.no provision for them when they are retired by reason of their services not being required.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think in that case they get a gratuity, and not a pension.
But they may have paid in more than the amount of the gratuity.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My recollection is that they get what they paid in, with some interest.
If that is so it is satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe if they are dismissed they do not get anything.
May I ask if the counting of service in the great war for pension purposes is a new principle being incorporated in the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a new principle in the mounted police act.

Formerly when persons
joined the police after having served in the great war, that service was not counted for pension, as I understand it, but it will be counted under this new legislation. Is this going to be a sort of blanket provision, taking in those who were members of the police force prior to the amalgamation of the customs preventive service, or will it deal only with those who are to benefit by this particular legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend probably knows that a great many members of the mounted police joined the forces and participated in the great war. Up until they left for the war their time counted for pension, out while they were away it did not count, and on their return a great many of them rejoined the police force. The provision is that such men who served in the great war shall be able to count the three or four years thus spent in connection with pension, and the same privilege will be given those in the preventive service. Any time they spent overseas will be counted towards pension, just as if they had served in the police force.

Perhaps I did not make myself quite clear. I quite understand the situation in connection with those mentioned by the minister, that is, men who prior to the

war were members of the mounted police. It would be a very curious anomaly indeed if the time they spent at the war could not be counted for pension; I think we all agree on that. But I was asking the minister whether or not the time served overseas by a recruit who may join to-day, or who joined t-wo or three years ago, will be counted with his police service, in connection with his pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The case could hardly
arise under the present regulations, because they provide that no one shall be taken in who is over twenty-eight years of age. A man who is twenty-eight years of age to-day would have been a very young man at the close of the war; he would not have been able to serve.

Did the same regulation
apply in the preventive service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, but the preventive
service would be included under this provision, and any member who served in the great war would be able to count that time.

I understand that civil
servants who served in the war had that time counted for pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.
If a member of the customs preventive service served during the war, and is now incorporated in the mounted police, his time in the servioe and his war service would both count for pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Now take the case of a
man who joined the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, say, in 1925 or 1926 when, so far as I know, the regulations were not so severe and when the age limit was not twenty-eight years. Would the time he served in the war be counted for pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, certainly.
That would not be so under the legislation previously in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. That will be provided for in the bill which I propose to introduce.
Then I want to congratulate the minister.

Under whose jurisdiction will the police in the provinces come? Will they report to and be directly controlled by the officials of the Dominion government

Royal Canadian Mounted Police
or the officials of the provincial government, or will they come under a dual control in respect of the different acts which they may enforce? That is, would they come directly under the control of the dominion in regard to the enforcement of purely federal laws, and would they report to and come under the control of the provincial authorities in respect of provincial matters?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They will be directly
under the control of their own officers, and under the immediate control of Major General MacBrien, the commissioner. My hon. friend will see under the act that for certain purposes the force is under the Department of Justice, and for the time being the Minister of Justice is designated as the minister in control. But in each of the provinces where the system is now in operation we have a divisional officer, a superintendent, who is *directly in touch with the attorney general of the province, and the administration of law is largely carried on through that superintendent .and the attorney general. The supreme control of the force, however, is certainly with the [DOT]commissioner at Ottawa.
But in the actual working out of the act the control, for ordinary every day purposes, will be divided in accordance with the particular law which may be enforced?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that is a fair statement of what is taking place.
Where will the deputy commissioner be located-in Ottawa or somewhere in the western provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think in Ottawa. I had a discussion with the commissioner to-day and he said that the pressure had been so great here that he would have to have someone with more authority than now existed and that the deputy commissioner would be stationed here with himself.
I think that is an additional plum.

Will the age regulation be observed in the transference of men from the provincial police to the Royal Canadian
service ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not as regards the men already in the service.

Regarding the division of work, and the men in the preventive service of the provincial police who have been taken in in each province, will there be a sharp division or will they work in cooperation? Are their duties the same? Will the duties of the provincial police be defined by the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They will be under one control, and I should think there would be cooperation in every respect between them; but that is a matter about which I could not give definite information.
What will become of the heads of the provincial police in each province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those who have been favourably reported on as good officers are retained.
In what capacity?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot tell; that will be under the control of the commissioner too,
I fancy.
Will they receive the same salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot say. They will be police force salaries.
What is the salary of the deputy commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has not been fixed; it will have to be fixed in the bill.

Where the mounted
police have taken over police duties in the provinces, which of the two governments will determine the number of police required for all
purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They have been determined by the provinces on the basis of a three-year agreement. They name the number and pay one thousand dollars per man.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Guthrie thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 63, to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 42, to amend the Criminal Code. (Trustees defined. Disposition of fines).
Criminal Code

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Payment of fines in Ontario to municipalities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I desire to withdraw this section. The circumstances, 'briefly, are these. Section 2 was placed in the bill at the request of the government of Ontario. The effect of passing the section would 'be to allow the government of Ontario to dispose of all fines which are recovered in that province, as is permitted in all the other provinces of Canada to-day. In 1922 the government of Ontario induced this parliament to pass a special clause applying only to Ontario, which provided that these fines should go back directly to the municipalities. I received a request early in the year, asking me to go back to the old system that prevailed prior to 1922, and allow the fines to go directly to the province, the province to deal with them. Since I introduced the bill I have received word from the attorney general of Ontario that he proposes during the summer or autumn to call a conference of the municipalities of Ontario in regard to this question. A great many of the municipalities are not agreeable to the section now proposed. He says he will confer with them, and he has asked me to withdraw this clause of the 'bill for the present session and will advise me at the next session whether the province of Ontario desires it. Under these circumstances, if the committee is agreeable, I would move that it be withdrawn.
. Mr. ELLIOTT: There is no relationship between the two sections of the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
None at all.
Motion agreed to and section withdrawn.
Bill as amended reported, read the third time and passed.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES

speechtext:
Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide that the governor in council, upon the recommendation of the Minister of the Interior may authorize the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of any sums of money received in connection with the administration of the natural

resources prior to the transfer thereof to the western provinces, which His Majesty is under any legal or equitable obligation to refund, and that an annual statement be laid before parliament of all moneys refunded hereunder.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Will the minister explain the resolution?

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
When the Department of the Interior was . administering the natural resources of the western provinces, the regulations and practice in many instances called for the payment of moneys to the department in advance of the granting of rights. In some cases the moneys were tendered as guarantee deposits; in other cases, as advance payments; in other cases, the regulations provided a drawback. In all these cases, it was customary to refund any over-payment as speedily as determined.
In addition to the foregoing, there were cases where settlers made improvements on homesteads which they afterwards abandoned. Re-entrants for the same land paid the department the value of the improvements and it was customary to refund this amount to the cancelled entrant as soon as it had been collected from the reentrant, provided the municipality in which the land was situated certified that no unpaid taxes had accrued meanwhile.
Again, under the authority of an order in council of May 29, 1925, certain regulations governing the conversion of patented preemptions or purchased homesteads into soldier grants were established. Under these regulations, which were subsequently continued, settlers who had paid in full or in part for their preemptions or purchased homesteads, and who were entitled to soldier grant entry by reason of their military service, were permitted to convert their preemption or purchased homestead, as the case might be, into a soldier grant and obtained a refund of the purchase price.
So long as the department was receiving the revenue from dominion lands administration, no question arose as to the policy followed consistently by succeeding administrations. The refunds were made from current revenue. However, with the passing of the control of the natural resources to the provinces, the source of revenue disappeared.
Generally speaking, the applications may be roughly classified as follows:
(a) Petroleum and natural gas prospecting permit deposits: in addition to the prescribed rental, each applicant for a permit was re-

Natural Resources
quired to make a deposit of forty cents an acre, which was returnable upon evidence being submitted that an equal expenditure had been incurred in prospecting operations on the location held under permit.
(b)	Dominion lands: when homesteaders gave assignments to railway companies for areas acquired for right-of-way, the railway company, at the request of the department, instead of paying the consideration money over to the entrant, forwarded it here to be held in trust, pending the issue of patent. When the department ascertains that the entrant has become entitled to patent, it has been the practice to refund the money to him.
(c)	Moneys paid to the department in connection with yearly licences and permits to cut timber on dominion lands: this department is holding certain sums which have been received in connection with the disposal of timber rights on dominion lands in the four western provinces, either in the form of deposits made as a guarantee that the permittee will pay the prescribed charges and conform with the timber regulations, or of credit balances which have arisen in favour of the permittee or berth-holder during the course of his operations.
(d)	Seed grain: an occasional settler who has paid an instalment on seed grain indebtedness charged against the land for which he obtained entry, upon abandoning such entry has been permitted to obtain a refund of the sum so paid by him.
(e)	Preemptions converted into soldier grants: the practice there has been as previously mentioned.
(f)	Improvements left on cancelled homesteads or leases: the explanation is the same as was given under another heading.
(g)	Soldier settler timber permits: refunds of dues paid in connection with settlers' timber permits on soldier settlement land from time to time as patents are issued by this department.
(h)	Timber permit issued-no timber cut: refunds of dues paid on timber uncut under permits issued prior to the transfer of the resources, as the refunds are applied for.
(i)	Grazing leases: moneys paid for improvements in connection with grazing leases which are refunded to the party who left the improvements on the land.
(j)	Hay permit refunds: where no hay has been cut or where amount covered by permit is not available.
The total amount applied for to date is $51,140.75, although that may not be the
total amount applied for as applications may come in now or later.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
The language of the
resolution is rather broad in the authorization it gives to the governor in council to pay sums of money which the crown is under any legal or equitable obligation to refund. Will the various cases which my hon. friend has mentioned, be indicated in the bill, or will it be rather in the nature of a blank cheque, leaving it to the discretion of the government as to whether the crown is under any equitable obligation to pay the sums which may be claimed from it?

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
The language of the bill
follows pretty much that of the resolution-

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: That is pretty broad.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: -but the intention is to continue to make payments out of the consolidated revenue fund on the authority of the governor in council on the same principle as that on which payments have been made, as a matter of legal right or of grace, during the past number of years. The hon. member will understand that these payments have been made for many years out of moneys which were received when the dominion was administering the resources and the department was in possession of current funds. Now that that revenue has dried up owing to the transfer of the resources, this simply gives the minister power, under authority of the governor in council, to make these payments out of the consolidated revenue whereas formerly they were made out of the current revenue of the department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: No power conferred under the bill to be founded on this resolution will be greater than that exercised by the minister before the resources were turned over, that is, the power conferred upon the governor in council will not be greater than that exercised by the governor in council heretofore.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: The power exercised by the minister is under what law?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
When the resources were administered by the dominion, the minister exercised his power through an order in council and returned moneys by order in council as regards claims that were sometimes equitable with respect to homesteads and matters of that kind, and sometimes purely legal. There is no longer a fund except the consolidated revenue fund out of which the moneys can be paid. This is to authorize the same order in council upon the recommendation of the minister for the payment of
Natural Resources

moneys that might be held in trust or otherwise on an order in council and that heretofore were paid out_ of departmental funds.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Will this
cover all claims originating prior to the return of the resources?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is intended, as the
minister has said, to cover those claims which have not yet been adjusted, but which must be settled in some way because they arose prior to the time the resources were turned over. The money is now in the possession of the dominion. In some instances a legal claim exists; in some cases it is purely equitable. This is to enable the minister now to deal with those moneys out of the consolidated revenue fund through an order in council just as heretofore he himself used to have an order in council passed and a cheque could be issued accordingly. That cannot be done except by the authority now conferred, owing to the resources themselves having been turned over to the provinces, and the moneys formerly in the departmental fund being in the consolidated revenue fund.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Is it proposed
that this legislation shall apply to the railway belt in British Columbia and the Peace River block?

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: It gives the minister power under the authority of the governor in council to make refunds out of consolidated revenue fund which were formerly made by the minister through order in council.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
And it would
apply to the railway lands in British Columbia?

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: Any individual heretofore entitled to a refund in connection with lands or grazing or hay or timber permits would still be entitled to it, and the minister under this legislation would be able to make such refund under the authority of the governor in council.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: What I have in mind is the case of a preemptor who took up a piece of land. On that land there was timber, and when he cut the timber and disposed of it he was obliged to pay a royalty on it. The royalty was imposed on the distinct understanding that when he had secured his patent the amount of the royalty would be refunded to the settler. They have had difficulty in British Columbia since the return of the natural resources in getting a refund, and I suppose that this legislation is to give the minister authority to pay back amounts of this nature. Is that correct?

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: As the question of interest has come up, I would ask if the department pays interest to a man where there has been delay for months or years in paying the principal?

subtopic: REFUND OF MONEY RECEIVED PRIOR TO TRANSFER TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
To the best of my knowledge there would be no interest paid to an individual. He would get his principal back without interest.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Murphy thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 64, to authorize the refund of mone3's received in connection with the administration of the natural resources.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: EASTERN BANK .OF CANADA BANK CIRCULATION REDEMPTION FUND-PAYMENT TO ESTATE OF THE LATE ANGUS MCLEAN

speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (for the Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That the Minister of Finance be authorized to pay to the executors of the estate of the late Angus McLean, of Bathurst, New Brunswick, the sum of $5,000, being the amount of the bank circulation redemption fund at the credit of the Eastern Bank of Canada, which was incorporated by chapter 28 of the statutes of 1928, but did not commence business.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EASTERN BANK .OF CANADA BANK CIRCULATION REDEMPTION FUND-PAYMENT TO ESTATE OF THE LATE ANGUS MCLEAN
speechtext:
There are a number of non-contentions resolutions and bills standing in the name of the Minister of Finance, none of which I would ask the house to consider if they dealt with controversial matters. This particular resolution is non-eontentious, perhaps the committee will deal with it.
Shortly, a bank was incorporated called the Eastern Bank of Canada, and into the bank circulation redemption fund there were paid certain sums of money, including $5,000 by the late Angus McLean. The bank did not function. All its bills have been paid and certificates to that effect have been given. Mr. McLean is dead and his executors are entitled to this money, but it requires a statute to take it out of the fund.

maintopic: EASTERN BANK .OF CANADA BANK CIRCULATION REDEMPTION FUND-PAYMENT TO ESTATE OF THE LATE ANGUS MCLEAN
speechtext: The bank was not incorporated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EASTERN BANK .OF CANADA BANK CIRCULATION REDEMPTION FUND-PAYMENT TO ESTATE OF THE LATE ANGUS MCLEAN
speechtext:
It was incorporated by this parliament.

Eastern Bank oj Canada

maintopic: EASTERN BANK .OF CANADA BANK CIRCULATION REDEMPTION FUND-PAYMENT TO ESTATE OF THE LATE ANGUS MCLEAN
speechtext: A bill was passed by the Senate and came to this house in 1929. Mr. McLean was not the original incorporator. Mr. Taylor was the promoter. The only question I want to ask is, have the interests of others been fully protected who were as deeply interested in this bank as Mr. McLean was when he was alive? Are they clear of all responsibility?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EASTERN BANK .OF CANADA BANK CIRCULATION REDEMPTION FUND-PAYMENT TO ESTATE OF THE LATE ANGUS MCLEAN
speechtext:
The moneys paid in were returned to everybody except Mr. McLean, and had he been alive the sum mentioned in the resolution would probably have been returned to him. With the lapse of time this money went into the fund, and it is now possible to withdraw it only by the authority of a statute. The necessary releases and so forth will be furnished to the minister before payment is made. The money is not that of the government; it belongs to Mr. McLean's estate.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Bennett thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 65 respecting the Eastern Bank of Canada.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
Mr. BENNETT moved the second reading of the bill.

maintopic: EASTERN BANK .OF CANADA BANK CIRCULATION REDEMPTION FUND-PAYMENT TO ESTATE OF THE LATE ANGUS MCLEAN
speechtext: By consent.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EASTERN BANK .OF CANADA BANK CIRCULATION REDEMPTION FUND-PAYMENT TO ESTATE OF THE LATE ANGUS MCLEAN
speechtext: This, of course, is being proceeded with now only by consent. Is the bill printed, Mr. Chairman?

maintopic: EASTERN BANK .OF CANADA BANK CIRCULATION REDEMPTION FUND-PAYMENT TO ESTATE OF THE LATE ANGUS MCLEAN
speechtext:
Yes, but not numbered.
On the preamble.
Mr. COOTE; What is the number of the bill?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER CONCERNING ATTENDANCE IN BERMUDA OF MEMBERS OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER CONCERNING ATTENDANCE IN BERMUDA OF MEMBERS OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it being nearly six
o'clock, I desire as a matter affecting the privileges of this house, to refer to an editorial appearing in the Ottawa Journal of Wednesday, April 27, 1932. The editorial is headed "A Nice Little Joy Ride." The last paragraph is as follows:
There will be hard cynical people, of course -perhaps some of them have been feeling the economy axe-who will complain; who will think this is just a nice joy-ride at the country's expense. And there may be some even who will wonder why the grand passion for economy didn't reach out to include votes for a Parliamentary Association to help some of its members golf amid zephyr breezes that kiss the breakers on coral reefs. But they really mustn't. Our tired legislators, and particularly those who have been attending the strenuous sessions of the Senate, need this little vacation; especially as they are going to kill two birds with one stone and help save the empire while saving themselves.
I may say that Bermuda sent invitations, through the Clerk of the House as secretary of the Empire Parliamentary Association, inviting a certain number of members of the Senate and the House of Commons to visit Bermuda at the expense of the government of that place. No money of this country has been voted for the purpose. The sum appearing in the estimates that is paid to the Empire Parliamentary Association is paid for publications and is remitted in its entirety to the secretary of the association for that purpose. It is wholly incorrect and absolutely unfair to say or suggest that those who have been selected, or have agreed to go to Bermuda as guests of the Bermuda government have been taking money from this country for that purpose. The report is as inaccurate as it possibly could be; it is unfair to this parliament and to the gentlemen who have gone from this chamber and the Senate to Bermuda. It is a little difficult to understand why such a statement should have been made.

subtopic: PRESS REFERENCES TO RELATIONS BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PRESS REFERENCES TO RELATIONS BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
have just been reading an editorial appearing in the Ottawa Journal of Wednesday, April 27, 1932, immediately below the one to which my right hon. friend has just referred. It may affect the privileges of the house, and certainly is a matter of personal privilege. The article is headed, "Mr. Bennett and Mr. King," and begins as follows:
According to despatches sent out to Winnipeg and Toronto papers, Premier Bennett and Mr. Mackenzie King have ceased to be on speaking terms, have no personal nor social contacts. This, if it be true, is a pity.
The article continues at some length. So far as I am concerned I was not aware that I had ceased to be on speaking terms with my right hon. friend. It is quite true I have not felt able to accept some of the invitations he has kindly extended, but beyond that I have not been aware of any personal difference with the Prime Minister.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRESS REFERENCES TO RELATIONS BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad the right hon. gentleman has made the observations to which we have just listened. I have had no occasion to speak to him and therefore I cannot be said not to be on speaking terms with him. The last occasion I had the opportunity of speaking to him I did not observe anything in his conduct which would indicate that he was unwilling to speak to me. Perhaps I spoke first on that occasion, but inasmuch as there have been very acute differences between us, in connection with which he said he would not accept any statement made by me, I assume the newspapers concluded that as a matter of intelligent discrimination I might decline to make any.
On motion of Mr. Bennett the house adjourned at 5.45 p.m.
Thursday, April 28, 1932
